newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada says two firms bid for satellite service.
newsitem.headline: Canada says two firms bid for satellite service.

text.p: Industry Canada on Tuesday said it received proposals from two companies to provide direct broadcast satellite services to Canadian consumers.
The companies who applied were Telesat Canada and Borealis Space Corp, the ministry said.
"The first step for Industry Canada will be to determine if the applications meet the criteria for "fast track" licensing," Industry Canada said in a statement.
But it said the call for applications will remain open until a decision is made.
On Monday, Telesat, 57 percent owned by BCE Inc, announced it had submitted a proposal in response to a call on November 7 from Industry Minister John Manley.
Manley's office had said companies would have until February 28 to submit their proposals.

But if a company already had a satellite or sufficient capacity to meet interim Canadian needs, it would be considered for fast-track licensing. Applications for the fast track were due on December 16.

Manley's decision to invite Canadian bids for the use of a Canadian orbital slot came after the U.S. Federal Communications Commission denied a bid by two U.S. companies to beam programs across North America through two satellites which were to be owned and operated by Telesat Canada.
Those two U.S. companies were TelQuest Ventures and Tele-Communications Inc.
In addition to BCE's 57 percent share, Telesat is also owned by Canadian phone companies and Spar Aerospace Ltd.
Expressvu Inc, partly owned by BCE, has regulatory approval to operate a satellite television service but has been stymied partly by lack of satellite capacity.
Power DirecTv, 80 percent owned by Power Corp of Canada, also won a license but decided against launching it at least for now.
A unit of Direct Choice T.V. Inc won a third license, and Tee-Comm Electronics Inc also filed for approval to launch a satellite service.
